_comment: The whole voiceover script. Each scene is a list of lines; each line is one caption and one voice clip. `speech` (optional) is what the voice says when it should differ from the caption. `pad` (optional) adds extra seconds after the line so an animation can finish. Scene ids must match SCENE_COMPONENTS in src/TransformerVideo.tsx.

lines.text: Chatbots, translators, code assistants: almost all of them run on the same design.
It's called the Transformer, introduced in 2017 in a paper titled “Attention Is All You Need”.
lines.speech: It's called the Transformer, introduced in 2017, in a paper titled: Attention Is All You Need.

lines.text: Let's build one up, piece by piece.
Earlier language models, called recurrent networks, read a sentence one word at a time.
Everything they knew had to squeeze into one memory vector, passed from word to word.
That was slow, because no step can start before the previous one ends. And early words fade away.
A Transformer takes in all the words at once, and lets every word look directly at every other word.
First, the text is split into tokens: words or pieces of words.
Each token has an ID number in a fixed vocabulary.
And each ID looks up a learned vector, called an embedding. In the original model it has 512 numbers.
lines.speech: And each ID looks up a learned vector, called an embedding. In the original model, it has five hundred and twelve numbers.

lines.text: During training, words used in similar ways end up with similar vectors.
But attention, as we'll see, has no built-in sense of order.
“Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” would look exactly the same.
lines.speech: Dog bites man, and man bites dog, would look exactly the same.

lines.text: So a positional encoding is added to each embedding: a pattern of waves that is unique for every position.
Fast waves tell nearby positions apart, slow waves tell far-apart ones apart.
Now the key idea. Take this sentence: what does “it” refer to?
lines.speech: Now the key idea. Take this sentence. What does the word “it” refer to?

lines.text: You know it's the animal, because animals get tired, not streets.
Attention lets the word “it” look at every other word, and give each one a weight.
Change one word to “wide”, and the attention moves to “street”.
The new vector for “it” is then a weighted mix of the words it attends to.
How are those weights computed? Each word makes three vectors from its embedding.
A query: what am I looking for?
A key: what do I contain?
And a value: what will I pass on, if someone attends to me?
Each is made by multiplying the embedding by a learned matrix: W Q, W K and W V.
lines.speech: Each is made by multiplying the embedding by a learned matrix: W Q, W K, and W V.

lines.text: A query that matches a key well gives a high score, like a search engine matching a request to page titles.
Here is the whole calculation, with real numbers, for a four-word sentence.
Step one: multiply every query by every key. This gives a grid of scores.
Step two: divide by the square root of the vector size, to keep the numbers in a sensible range.
Step three: softmax turns each row into weights that are positive and add up to one.
Step four: each word's output is the weighted sum of all the value vectors.
That's it. The whole of attention is one line: softmax of Q K transpose over root d, times V.
lines.speech: That's it. The whole of attention is one line: softmax of Q K transpose, over root d, times V.

lines.text: One attention pattern can only capture one kind of relationship at a time.
So the Transformer runs several attention heads side by side, each with its own query, key and value matrices.
One head might link each word to the previous one, another pronouns to nouns, another verbs to their objects.
Their outputs are joined together and mixed by one more matrix. The original model used 8 heads.
lines.speech: Their outputs are joined together, and mixed by one more matrix. The original model used eight heads.

lines.text: Attention is the heart of a Transformer block, but not the whole of it.
The attention output is added back onto its input: a residual connection, so information can skip ahead.
Then layer normalization keeps the numbers well scaled.
Next, a feed-forward network processes each word on its own: attention mixes between words, the feed-forward thinks within each one.
Another residual and normalization, and the block is complete. Vectors in, same-shaped vectors out.
Because the output has the same shape as the input, blocks can be stacked.
The original Transformer used 6. GPT-3 uses 96.
lines.speech: The original Transformer used six. GPT three uses ninety six.

lines.text: Layer by layer, each word's vector is refined: from the word itself, to its grammar, to its meaning in context.
The original Transformer was built for translation, with two stacks.
The encoder reads the whole source sentence, and every word may look at every other.
The decoder writes the translation one word at a time. Through cross-attention, its queries look at the encoder's keys and values.
Later models kept just one half: BERT is an encoder, GPT is a decoder, and T5 keeps both.
lines.speech: Later models kept just one half. BERT is an encoder. GPT is a decoder. And T five keeps both.

lines.text: A GPT-style model generates text by predicting the next token.
lines.speech: A GPT style model generates text, by predicting the next token.

lines.text: While training, a word must not peek at the words after it. A causal mask blocks them before the softmax.
At the end, the last word's vector is turned into a score for every token in the vocabulary.
Softmax turns the scores into probabilities, and one token is picked.
It's added to the input, and the whole process repeats, one token at a time.
Why did Transformers win? First, they process all words in parallel, which suits GPUs perfectly.
Second, any two words are just one step apart, however far apart they are in the text.
Third, they keep getting better as they get bigger: from 65 million parameters in 2017 to 175 billion in GPT-3.
lines.speech: Third, they keep getting better as they get bigger: from sixty five million parameters in 2017, to a hundred and seventy five billion in GPT three.

lines.text: The price: every word attends to every word, so the cost grows with the square of the length.
To recap: tokens become vectors, plus a sense of position.
Attention lets every word gather information from every other word, through queries, keys and values.
Wrap it with residuals, normalization and a feed-forward network, stack it many times, and you have a Transformer.
